idiom_name: java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue via a Scala wrapper returning Either/Boolean
implementation_notes: On the JVM the pattern is the JDK's bounded queue driven from Scala: ArrayBlockingQueue(capacity) is a classic bounded buffer where put blocks, offer returns false, offer(e, timeout, unit) waits up to a bound and add throws IllegalStateException, so the policy is chosen by the method. When the queue sits behind a ThreadPoolExecutor, the RejectedExecutionHandler classes (Abort, CallerRuns, Discard, DiscardOldest) lift that choice into a replaceable object. The idiomatic Scala touch is to make the refusal part of the type - a Boolean or Either[Full, Unit] from a tryOffer method - so callers cannot ignore the shed decision the way a bare Unit-returning call invites.
code_sketch:
val q = new java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue[Msg](10_000)   // classic bounded buffer
def offer(m: Msg): Either[String, Unit] =                          // the refusal is in the type
  if (q.offer(m)) Right(()) else Left("buffer full")
val pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(8, 8, 0L, SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue[Runnable](1_000),
  new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy)
pitfalls: Scala's own mutable collections are neither thread-safe nor bounded: using mutable.Queue as 'the buffer' loses the bound and the atomicity in one step.
put/take block a real thread (possibly a ForkJoinPool worker); in cats-effect/ZIO/akka code that blocking call must be moved to a dedicated pool or replaced by a demand-driven queue.
JVM queues reject null elements, so a null 'empty' sentinel silently becomes an exception instead of a value - use Option or a dedicated empty type.

variants.name: Akka/Pekko Streams buffer with an overflow strategy
variants.implementation_notes: Stream-based Scala names the decision as a strategy value: .buffer(1000, OverflowStrategy.dropHead) inserts an explicitly sized buffer between stages, where backpressure propagates the shortage upstream and the drop strategies discard deliberately - dropTail loses the youngest waiting element, dropHead the oldest. The same documentation shows the catch that makes this variant worth stating separately: every asynchronous operator already carries its own internal input buffer (16 elements by default), so a pipeline that never calls buffer() can still queue material and distort latency measurements. Use the strategy form when the queue exists to decouple pipeline stages; keep the JDK queue when consumers are unrelated threads.
variants.idiom_name: flow.buffer(size, OverflowStrategy.backpressure | dropHead | dropTail | dropNew | fail)
variants.code_sketch:
Source(jobs)
  .buffer(1_000, OverflowStrategy.dropHead)    // capacity + the decided outcome
  .mapAsync(8)(process)
  .runWith(Sink.ignore)
pitfalls: dropHead and dropTail are relative to the buffer and easy to invert: choosing the wrong one changes which work is sacrificed without any error.
Internal input buffers of asynchronous operators (16 by default) are invisible in the code and are a common mis-attribution when latency is investigated.
OverflowStrategy.fail turns overload into a stream failure: deliberate, but it needs a supervision/restart policy or the stage dies on the first surge.
